# Underwater Light Rays — Remotion project

Two procedural underwater compositions, each in two versions, authored at
**3840×2160 (4K UHD), 30 fps**. Everything is generated by WebGL 2 fragment
shaders; there are no image or video assets.

| Composition ID                    | Reference                    | Length              | Version |
| --------------------------------- | ---------------------------- | ------------------- | ------- |
| `Comp1-DeepRays-V1-Match`         | Ref 1 — deep ocean rays      | 601 frames (20.033 s) | Matches the reference: locked-off camera |
| `Comp1-DeepRays-V2-CameraMove`    | Ref 1                        | 601 frames (20.033 s) | Alternative **camera movement**: tilt-up/pan reveal towards the light with a gentle roll and particle parallax |
| `Comp2-SurfaceRays-V1-Match`      | Ref 2 — surface from below   | 300 frames (10.000 s) | Matches the reference: clear tropical blue |
| `Comp2-SurfaceRays-V2-GoldenHour` | Ref 2                        | 300 frames (10.000 s) | Alternative **colour palette**: golden-hour amber surface sinking into indigo |

Reference lengths are 20.04 s and 10.01 s. At 30 fps those are 601.2 and
300.3 frames, so the compositions use the nearest whole frame count (always
within one frame, < 33 ms, of the reference).

## Requirements

- Node.js 20.19+ / 22.13+ / 24+
- A Chromium that Remotion can drive. Remotion downloads its own Chrome
  Headless Shell on first render. (In sandboxes that block that download,
  `remotion.config.ts` reuses a Playwright headless shell if one exists at
  `/opt/pw-browsers/...`.)
- WebGL 2. `remotion.config.ts` sets the OpenGL renderer to `angle`, which uses
  the GPU when available and falls back to SwiftShader (CPU) otherwise. If you
  see "WebGL 2 is not available", add `--gl=swangle` to the render command.

## Setup

```bash
npm install
```

## Preview

```bash
npm run dev          # Remotion Studio
```

## Render

4K masters (3840×2160, H.264, 30 fps) into `out/`:

```bash
npm run render:4k            # all four
npm run render:4k:c1v1       # just one (c1v1, c1v2, c2v1, c2v2)
```

1080p deliverables (the same 4K composition rendered at `--scale=0.5`, which
supersamples the shader and downsizes to 1920×1080):

```bash
npm run render:1080p         # all four
npm run render:1080p:c2v2    # just one
```

Or directly with the Remotion CLI:

```bash
npx remotion render Comp1-DeepRays-V1-Match out/comp1-v1-4k.mp4
npx remotion render Comp1-DeepRays-V1-Match out/comp1-v1-1080p.mp4 --scale=0.5
```

Codec (H.264), pixel format (yuv420p), CRF 16 and JPEG frame quality are set
in `remotion.config.ts`. On a CPU-only machine expect roughly 2 s per 4K frame;
with a GPU it is far faster.

## Project layout

```
remotion.config.ts       render settings (codec, quality, GL backend)
src/index.ts             entry point
src/Root.tsx             registers the four 4K compositions
src/constants.ts         resolution, fps and durations
src/DeepRays.tsx         composition 1 (light pulse + camera animation)
src/SurfaceRays.tsx      composition 2 (palettes)
src/gl/ShaderCanvas.tsx  WebGL 2 full-screen shader renderer driven by useCurrentFrame()
src/shaders/common.ts    GLSL noise / fbm / dither helpers
src/shaders/deepRays.ts  composition 1 fragment shader
src/shaders/surfaceRays.ts composition 2 fragment shader
```

Every frame is a pure function of the frame number (no `Math.random`, no
wall-clock time), so renders are deterministic and parallelise safely.
